scoreRule: 1 point per correct MC item; 10 points maximum; local provisional grade only

tabs.title: Cases and Conditional Evidence
tabs.description: Assess how examples qualify general claims.

tabs.title: Institutional Judgement
tabs.description: Reason about evidence, uncertainty and policy choices.

questions.q: What is lost when planetary defence is presented chiefly as a struggle against an enemy?
choices: The fact that physical bodies obey observable forces becomes irrelevant.
The need for political choices disappears from public discussion.
Asteroid trajectories can no longer be expressed numerically.
Attention shifts from conditional scientific knowledge to a misleading dramatic conflict.
questions.explanation: The opening criticises a cinematic metaphor that conceals the slower scientific work required.

questions.q: Why does the author resist treating high numerical precision as evidence of complete knowledge?
choices: The calculations necessarily contain random errors too large to evaluate.
Observed samples are shaped by detection biases and may exclude unobserved objects.
Infrared telescopes measure only the temperature of the Sun.
Probability theory cannot be applied to astronomical observations.
questions.explanation: Paragraph two distinguishes precise orbit solutions from completeness of the observed catalogue.

questions.q: How can a rise in a preliminary risk estimate be consistent with responsible reasoning?
choices: New observations may constrain possible trajectories in a way that temporarily raises the calculated chance.
Institutional hesitation automatically improves astronomical accuracy.
The object's gravitational forces change according to media coverage.
The first calculation must have been intentionally misleading.
questions.explanation: The text explains why a narrower set of admissible orbits can yield changing risk estimates.

questions.q: What does the later observational history of Apophis chiefly demonstrate?
choices: An initially alarming estimate must always be ignored.
The 2029 pass was already understood as harmless in 2004.
Revised evidence can transform an apparent threat into a well-characterised research opportunity.
Radar observations are useful only for objects visible to the naked eye.
questions.explanation: The text traces how observations ruled out impacts and reframed the close passage as an opportunity.

questions.q: Why is DART's successful impact described as a conditional engineering lesson?
choices: DART's target was selected after an unavoidable collision with Earth.
The collision showed that every asteroid responds identically.
The experiment proved detection systems could be eliminated.
The result depends on target structure, available warning and a measurable change in future position.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph stresses the context-dependent nature of a demonstrated kinetic deflection.

questions.q: What is the force of comparing a solid rock with a loosely bound collection of fragments?
choices: It suggests that loosely bound targets cannot follow an orbit.
It challenges the assumption that one impact result transfers unchanged to every target.
It proves that all planetary-defence experiments are unreliable.
It reduces the importance of detecting objects early.
questions.explanation: The comparison shows why physical structure affects the outcome of an intervention.

questions.q: What makes rare-impact preparedness especially difficult to justify in public policy?
choices: Every low-probability risk can be forecast with perfect accuracy.
International cooperation is impossible for infrequent events.
Its benefits are largely invisible and compete with urgent demands for resources.
Observation has no measurable scientific value.
questions.explanation: The author acknowledges both opportunity costs and the difficulty of demonstrating success through disasters that do not occur.

questions.q: A government demands perfectly certain forecasts before funding asteroid surveys. Why is that reasoning circular?
choices: Better forecasts depend on the observations the unfunded surveys would provide.
Asteroid detection becomes unnecessary once a government accepts uncertainty.
Scientific measurements are never relevant to public decisions.
Funding alone guarantees that no asteroid will reach Earth.
questions.explanation: The conclusion argues that uncertainty does not justify withholding investment in observation.

questions.q: What standard of institutional authority does the author ultimately endorse?
choices: A record of never retracting an earlier statement.
Inspectable assumptions and willingness to revise decisions as evidence changes.
A promise to eliminate scientific uncertainty.
The largest possible number of public reassurances.
questions.explanation: The final sentence ties trust to accessible assumptions and revisability rather than pretended certainty.

questions.q: What practical distinction follows from separating scientific investigation from political action?
choices: Any object on a near-Earth orbit must trigger immediate evacuation.
Political decisions should ignore scientific probabilities.
Scientists should not publish observations before government approval.
The evidence sufficient to monitor an asteroid need not yet justify an emergency response.
questions.explanation: The opening distinguishes a scientific reason to investigate from a political reason to act.
